vendor-claim.corrections: 1) MISSED TREZOR PRECEDENT for proposal item (2) ('tail required to be 0xFF'): the improvement credits only Krux, but Trezor already ships exactly this. core/embed/sec/image/image.c:469-500 check_image_contents(): after hashing hdr->codelen it sets end_offset = flash_area_get_size(area) and requires every remaining byte to equal the first padding byte, which must be 0xFF (firmware) or 0x00 (bootloader) — commit 02f34a2748 (2023-10-25) 'feat(core/bootloader): check firmware padding'. It runs in the boardloader for the bootloader area (boardloader/main.c:301) and in the bootloader for firmware (bootloader/fw_check.c:150). Note Trezor CHECKS the padding rather than hashing it; Krux hashes the whole region. pq1's proposal is therefore parity with Trezor (padding check variant) and with Krux (hash variant), not a Krux-only idea. 2) ATTACK-CLASS ORIGIN: the rationale attributes the compressible-firmware bypass to Donjon vs Trezor; the cited Ledger URL does support that ('security depends on the firmware being hard to compress ... avoiding leaving any blank space in flash'), but the original MCU-firmware-check bypass against a hardware wallet is Rashid 2018 vs Ledger Nano S (saleemrashid.com/2018/03/20/breaking-ledger-security-model/), which explicitly REJECTED compression ('To use a compression algorithm such as DEFLATE or LZMA would be impossible') and instead reused duplicated compiler intrinsics in the bootloader to reconstruct a genuine image for the SE. Ledger's LSB-005 later argued insufficient free space 'even after compression' as a defence — i.e. Ledger also treats free flash space as the attacker's budget. 3) THREAT-MODEL SCOPING (not a refutation): both the Rashid and Donjon bypasses work because the ATTACKER-CONTROLLED code computes/streams the hash. In pq1 the FSBL hashes from flash itself, so an unmeasured tail only matters (a) pre-RDP-2 (transit, where the FSBL itself is replaceable anyway), (b) as a staging area reachable via a bug in the authentic image, or (c) for the secure-world advisory measured_boot row. fw_update BEGIN already erases the WHOLE slot (secure/src/hw/flash.rs:1366-1386 erase_slot over all secure+NS pages) so the tail is erased by construction after an update; COMMIT (fw_update/verify.rs:41-110) hashes only received_secure/received_nonsecure and does not verify the tail. 4) SOURCE QUALITY: the TCHES link is Bozzato/Focardi/Palmarini 2019 'Shaping the Glitch: Optimizing Voltage Fault Injection Attacks' (TCHES 2019(2):199-224) — a generic V-FI firmware-extraction paper on STM32/TI/Renesas; it supports the general glitch threat but says nothing about option bytes, OEM keys, or slot tails. The Ledger URL is a Ledger blog about attacking Trezor's STM32F4 (Safe 3), not a description of Ledger's own architecture; it supports the 'blank space in flash' rationale only. 5) MINOR: Trezor's option_bytes_check_oem_keys runs only in the reprogram path (option_bytes.c:261), not on every boot when the profile already matches; Trezor's wipe-on-mismatch is a BHK regeneration (secret_bhk_regenerate), which pq1's page-125 wipe-flag analogue should be compared against (pq1 has a BHK axis too). Trezor fires this on ANY mismatch with no two-pass/persistence gate (main.c:325), so the improvement's F-2 two-pass requirement is stricter than the vendor precedent.

feasible.reason: The load-bearing half of IMP-06 is sound and firmware-only. RM0456 §7.6 confirms the threat and the defence exactly as proposed: OEM2KEY is writable at RDP 0 (so a transit attacker can plant it on the RDP-0 ship image), an OEM2LOCK=1 device at RDP-2 regresses to RDP-1 WITHOUT erasing application code, and the only observable is FLASH_NSSR.OEMxLOCK (keys read as zero); writing both key registers to all-ones at RDP-0 in the same OPTSTRT batch as RDP=0xCC is the documented un-set and is precisely what Trezor's option_bytes.c:219-222 does on the same silicon. The repo state is as the proposal says: `oem_locks_absent` and `wrp1a_covers_fsbl` fail closed behind `OEM_LOCK_MASK_PINNED=false` / `WRP1A_MASK_PINNED=false`, so the production profile cannot pass at all today, which makes (1) critical-path for rdp2-self-lock regardless of the threat and justifies P1. Whole-window hashing (2) is realisable (FSBL already has the HW HASH driver via `hw-sha256` default; fw_update erases the slot at BEGIN so the tail is 0xFF by construction) and the wipe escalation (4) has Trezor precedent. No hardware change is needed. Items (3) and (4) however contain design holes as written (see corrections): the FSBL has no flash-write path by design, a flag-then-halt in the FSBL is never consumed, OBLRSTF refusal without RMVF is a permanent brick lever, and the Donjon compression rationale does not apply to an FSBL-measured image. These are fixable corrections, not a bypass of the stated threat, so not refuted.
feasible.corrections: (a) Bit positions: the repo's `OEM1LOCK=1<<26 / OEM2LOCK=1<<27` (shared/src/lockdown.rs:278-279) and the proposal's "OEM lock bits 26/27" are the unpinned guess and are WRONG. RM0456 §7.9 FLASH_NSSR and CMSIS stm32u585xx.h:8668-8672 give OEM1LOCK=bit 18, OEM2LOCK=bit 19 of FLASH_NSSR (offset 0x20, not OPTSR). The silicon pin will move them; keep the fail-closed gate until the positive detection is run. (b) "Invisible to the SWD dump" is overstated: the key VALUES are write-only, but FLASH_NSSR.OEMxLOCK is readable over SWD at RDP-0, so the public connect-under-reset verification in invariant #10 should ALSO check NSSR bits 18/19 — a doc/tooling addition cheaper than any firmware. (c) RM0456 is internally inconsistent on OEM-key write levels (Table note at RM text line ~9471 says "OEM2 RDP=1 only"; §7.6 at ~21593-21596 says RDP 0 or 0.5). The §7.6 text plus Trezor's RDP-0→RDP-2 batch both support the proposal, but the Phase-A write MUST check OPTWERR after OPTSTRT and verify NSSR OEMxLOCK clear on the post-launch boot, and the silicon pin must include "write 0xFFFFFFFF at RDP-0 clears a planted lock bit", not just "a planted key trips the predicate". Note RM: keys must not be all-1 or all-0 — all-ones is the un-set encoding. (d) Item (4) as written is a no-op: the FSBL has NO production flash-write path (fsbl/src/marker.rs:1-8 states the design forbids it; `stage-marker` is bench-only), and even if it armed the page-125 wipe flag, the consumer is the secure world (dual_se.rs), which never runs while the FSBL keeps halting on the same persistent mismatch — the wipe never executes. To be real, the FSBL must either erase page 126 (DHUK-wrapped BHK) + page 127 (PBS salt/journal) itself — which effectively destroys both seed halves' access paths without an SE driver and fits the FSBL budget — or branch into the secure world with a wipe directive. Either is a deliberate relaxation of the "FSBL owns no flash mutation" posture and needs an owner decision + the WRP/geometry gate ordering. Also "Phase-A profile mismatch after RDP-2" does not exist: `run_pre_lock_and_maybe_lock` returns immediately at RDP-2 (first_boot/mod.rs:175-178); post-lock the only profile check is FSBL tz-1 (fsbl/src/main.rs:243-252). (e) Wipe-on-mismatch only raises cost: the glitch outcome that matters (latched RDP reads <2 → debug opens) lets the attacker connect-under-reset and halt the core before the FSBL executes a single instruction, so no FSBL-resident wipe fires. Trezor has the same limitation; call it parity, not a defence. SRAM_RST/SRAM2_RST (#82, "F9") is the cheaper lever for the SRAM-residue half of that scenario. (f) Item (3) is low value and a brick lever: OBLRSTF is set only by an OBL_LAUNCH-induced reset, which after RDP-2 merely reloads frozen bytes (NS can trigger it via NSCR as a DoS — it gains nothing), and a glitched option-byte load at POR sets no flag. Refusing to branch on IWDG/WWDG without clearing RMVF makes any watchdog bite a permanent no-boot (flags are sticky until software clears them), and clearing them in the FSBL starves secure/src/reset_cause.rs, which reads RCC_CSR at top of boot. If kept: read, pass the cause to the secure world (e.g. a register/SRAM word), never halt on it. (g) Rationale correction: the Donjon compression bypass defeats a SELF-ATTESTED firmware hash; pq1's FSBL row is measured by WRP-frozen code, so it is not affected, and the secure-world `firmware_hash()` row is already documented as self-attested (measured-boot.md:130-133) — a compromised secure world can lie regardless of the tail. The genuine gain of (2) is denying a pre-staged executable payload region to a future memory-safety exploit, plus closing any data the firmware reads from outside `nonsecure_len` (check whether the ui-px atlas at ATLAS_SLOT_OFFSET=0x1000 of the NS slot falls inside the manifest-declared NS length; if not it is a concrete unmeasured-tail consumer today, mitigated only by the secure-image SHA-256 pin). Random-fill-and-pin (Krux) is incompatible with the vendor-signed manifest hash; use 0xFF tail only. (h) Timing: the "4 s window" framing is wrong — the fingerprint hold is a deliberate pause (10 s per owner decision 2026-09-16; CLAUDE.md's 4 s is stale), not a budget the hash competes with. With software SHA-256 at HSI16 (1.167 s for 385,568 B), hashing the full 475,136+524,288 B windows costs ~3.0 s (+1.8 s); with the now-wired HW HASH it is well under 1 s. Cost M is right; the silicon pin for WRP1A (UNLOCK bit 31 clear is permanent) is the only step that consumes a board.
